challenges.title: Low-poly mug
challenges.description: Model a coffee mug to spec: 9-11 cm tall, 800 faces or fewer, no n-gons. Free rubric, free topology check in your browser, AI review for $9.
brief: Model a plain coffee mug: a round body with real wall thickness, a flat base, a rolled or squared rim and a handle that joins the body cleanly at both ends.
Keep it light. The whole mug fits in 800 faces with no n-gons, and at least 85% of the faces are quads. Make it watertight: no open edges, no holes where the handle meets the body.
Build it at real-world scale: 9 to 11 cm tall, with the body about 8 cm across. Export it as OBJ with triangulation off so your quads stay quads.

challenges.title: Rounded cube, holding edges
challenges.summary: 8 cm cube, crisp edges under subdivision, <= 600 faces
challenges.description: Model an 8 cm cube that keeps crisp, evenly rounded edges under subdivision, using support loops only. Free topology check, AI review for $9.
brief: Model a cube about 8 cm on each side that stays a cube when subdivided: every edge rounds by the same small radius, the faces stay flat and the corners stay tidy.

Hold the edges with support loops (edge loops placed close to each edge), not with creases or bevel weights, so the shape lives in the topology itself. Export the cage (Subdivision modifier off), all quads.
Keep it under 600 faces, with no n-gons and no triangles. Each corner meets in a clean three-edge pole.

challenges.title: Bouncing ball
challenges.summary: 3 bounces, 48-96 frames at 24 fps, side view
challenges.description: Animate a ball dropping and bouncing three times with decay, squash and stretch: 48-96 frames at 24 fps. Free contact sheets, AI review for $9.
brief: Animate a ball dropping from the top of the frame and bouncing three times, losing height on every bounce until it settles or rolls out.
Show the physics: the ball slows into each apex and speeds into each contact, squashes on contact and stretches on the fast frames around it, and its path makes clean, decaying arcs.
Keep the camera still and side-on, the ball fully in frame, 48 to 96 frames at 24 fps. Playblast to MP4 (H.264) or a PNG sequence.

reference.alt: Reference motion diagram for Bouncing ball: three decaying arcs from left to right, with spacing dots close together at each apex and far apart near each contact, and frame ticks under the floor line.

spec_list: Three bounces, each lower than the last
Squash on contact, stretch on the fast frames
Still, side-on camera; ball fully in frame
Export: H.264 MP4 or a PNG sequence

rubric.good: Each bounce takes less time than the one before; the ball hangs at each apex and is quick through each contact.

descriptors.10: Bounce durations shrink steadily and feel like gravity.
descriptors.7: Mostly right, with one bounce too long or too even.
descriptors.4: Bounces take about the same time, so the ball feels weightless or mechanical.
descriptors.0: No sense of gravity in the timing.

rubric.title: Spacing
rubric.good: Positions bunch up near each apex and spread out near each contact (slow in, slow out at the top; fast at the bottom).

descriptors.7: Easing present but uneven on one bounce.
descriptors.4: Even spacing for much of the clip.
descriptors.0: Spacing contradicts the motion, such as slowing into the floor.

descriptors.10: Squash on every contact and stretch on fast frames, with volume kept.

descriptors.4: Only one of squash or stretch, or the ball visibly changes volume.

rubric.good: The path forms clean parabolic arcs that lose height on every bounce; no wobble or sudden direction change in the air.

descriptors.4: Pointed or lumpy arcs, or bounces that do not decay.

challenges.description: Animate a bowling ball and a beach ball dropped side by side so each one's weight shows in timing alone: 72-120 frames at 24 fps. AI review for $9.
brief: Animate two balls of the same size dropped from the same height, side by side: a heavy bowling ball and a light beach ball.
Tell the weight with timing and spacing alone. The bowling ball falls fast, hits hard and barely bounces; the beach ball floats, bounces several times and drifts before it settles.
Still side-on camera, both balls fully in frame, 72 to 120 frames at 24 fps.

challenges.title: Pendulum follow-through
challenges.summary: Pendulum with a trailing tail, 48-96 frames at 24 fps
challenges.description: Animate a swinging pendulum with a flexible tail that drags and overlaps: 48-96 frames at 24 fps. Free contact sheets, AI review for $9.
brief: Animate a pendulum swinging from a fixed pivot, with a flexible tail (three or more joints, or a ribbon) hanging from the weight.

The pendulum eases at each end of its swing and is fastest at the bottom. The tail lags behind the weight, keeps moving after the weight changes direction and settles in a wave, never moving as one stiff piece.
Still side-on camera, 48 to 96 frames at 24 fps, at least two full swings.

reference.alt: Reference motion diagram for Pendulum follow-through: a pivot with a pendulum arc, spacing dots close at both ends of the arc, and the tail's trailing curve lagging behind the weight at each extreme.

spec_list: Ease at each extreme, fastest at the bottom
Tail of three or more joints that drags and overlaps
Export: H.264 MP4 or a PNG sequence

challenges.title: Flour sack jump
challenges.summary: Anticipation, jump, landing: 48-96 frames at 24 fps
challenges.description: Animate a flour sack that anticipates, jumps and lands with weight: 48-96 frames at 24 fps, side view. Free contact sheets, AI review for $9.
brief: Animate a flour sack (a sack shape with two top corners, no face or limbs) crouching, jumping forward and landing.

Sell it with pose and weight: a clear anticipation crouch that squashes the sack, a stretch on take-off, a readable shape at the top of the arc, and a landing that absorbs the weight before it settles.
Still side-on camera, 48 to 96 frames at 24 fps.

Sack shape only: no face or limbs

challenges.title: Walk cycle
challenges.description: Animate a 24-frame walk cycle in side view: contact, down, passing and up poses with clean arcs. 24-48 frames at 24 fps. AI review for $9.
brief: Animate a walk cycle in place, side view, on any simple biped rig: one full cycle in 24 frames (two steps of 12), rendered once or twice through.
Hit the four classic poses on each step: contact, down, passing and up. The hips rise and fall, the arms swing opposite to the legs, and nothing pops when the cycle loops.
Still side-on camera, the whole body in frame, 24 to 48 frames at 24 fps.

reference.alt: Reference motion diagram for Walk cycle: four stick-figure poses in a row, contact, down, passing and up, with the hip height marked by a wavy line and the arm swing opposite to the legs.

One cycle = 24 frames, a step every 12
Contact, down, passing and up on each step
Opposite arm swing; hips rise and fall
Loops without a pop; still side-on camera

challenges.title: Head turn with anticipation
challenges.summary: Head turn with a blink, 48-72 frames at 24 fps
challenges.description: Animate a head turn with anticipation, a blink and overlap: 48-72 frames at 24 fps. Free contact sheets, AI review for $9.
brief: Animate a character's head turning from looking at the camera to looking off to one side, about 90 degrees.
Add a small anticipation dip before the turn, ease in and out of the move, a blink during the turn (the classic way to sell a change of thought) and a little overlap as the head settles.
Still camera framing head and shoulders, 48 to 72 frames at 24 fps. Any simple rigged head works; a sphere with eyes is fine.

reference.alt: Reference motion diagram for Head turn with anticipation: a top view of a head with an arc from facing front to facing right, a small dip before the turn, and the blink marked at the middle of the arc.

spec_list: Ease in and out; a small overshoot and settle
